title: A Caption That Survives the Crop
hypothesis: Can provenance remain legible as visual structure when an interactive composition is cropped away from its original interface?

variables.changed: The visible frame crops from full study to book spread, archive thumbnail, and caption-only states.
variables.constants: Same typographic sheet, same question, same provenance strip, same controls.
variables.challenge: If readers cannot recover the question, method boundary, and source path after the crop, the caption is still metadata rather than structure.

research.title: Using container scroll-state queries
research.use: Frames scroll and crop as states a component can respond to, suggesting that contextual position can become a design material.
research.limitation: Documentation of a web platform feature; not evidence that audiences understand provenance better.

research.title: CSS scroll-state()
research.use: Identified a current move away from JavaScript-only scroll awareness toward state-aware CSS and progressive enhancement.
research.limitation: Supplier documentation; browser support and design adoption are not universal.

research.title: Inbox: Muriel Cooper's Information Landscapes
research.use: Used Cooper's movement from publication design into computer-based information landscapes as precedent for treating context and navigation as graphic material.
research.limitation: Museum summary of an exhibition; it does not specify this experiment's caption method or prove comprehension.

research.title: Understanding Success Criterion 2.4.7: Focus Visible
research.use: The frame controls remain keyboard operable and visibly focused so cropping can be explored without pointer-only interaction.
research.limitation: Focus visibility alone does not verify screen reader order, touch ergonomics, or reader interpretation.

candidateScoring.scale: 1-10, subjective selection only; not measured improvement

candidates.title: A Caption That Survives the Crop
candidates.reason: Extends Day004's concern with state into publication provenance without reusing proof typography; strong fit for the future book.

candidates.title: A Source That Refuses the Footnote
candidates.reason: Good editorial premise, but risks becoming static annotation rather than interactive structure.

candidates.title: The Image Forgets Its Interface
candidates.reason: Strong title and argument, weaker direct affordance for touch and keyboard.

candidates.title: A Thumbnail With a Memory
candidates.reason: Clear archive relevance, but thumbnail scale alone may overdetermine the interaction.

candidates.title: Citation as Gravity
candidates.reason: Visual force field is appealing but may become decorative physics.

candidates.title: The Footnote Moves First
candidates.reason: Elegant, but too close to conventional marginalia.

candidates.title: Portable Context
candidates.reason: Conceptually precise but visually bland unless overbuilt.

candidates.title: A Caption Becomes a Ruler
candidates.reason: Useful print metaphor, but measurement could introduce meaningless numbers.

candidates.title: The Crop Has Ethics
candidates.reason: Strong writing direction, but title may overpower the visual experiment.

candidates.title: Metadata With a Spine
candidates.reason: Book-relevant metaphor, but less immediately understandable on screen.

selectedReason: The selected concept turns citation and limitation into a visible strip that travels through crop states, directly supporting the book archive goal.
strongestAlternative: A Source That Refuses the Footnote may become a future comparison if a more essay-like page is needed.
interaction: Switch between crop contexts, toggle provenance, and use arrow/Home/End keys to test what remains readable.
performance: No external assets, no animation loop, no network calls, no storage.
